question: An investor holds 50 stocks across 10 sectors. They add 10 more. By approximately how much does portfolio risk decrease?
before: Most unsystematic risk is eliminated by 20–30 well-diversified stocks. Going from 50 to 60 stocks reduces risk by a tiny amount — the portfolio is already well-diversified. The marginal benefit declines sharply after ~25–30 stocks.
after:
Concept: Diversification benefit is the reduction in portfolio risk (measured by standard deviation) as unsystematic risk is eliminated by adding uncorrelated assets. The magnitude of this benefit diminishes as portfolio size increases because most unsystematic risk is captured early; systematic risk cannot be eliminated through diversification.

Step-by-step: The investor starts with 50 stocks across 10 sectors. Adding 10 more stocks (a 20% increase in number) brings the total to 60. Empirical research shows that approximately 90% of diversification benefit is achieved with 20–30 well-selected stocks. At 50 stocks, the portfolio is already highly diversified with minimal unsystematic risk remaining. Adding 10 more stocks captures negligible additional unsystematic risk reduction because the portfolio has already moved past the steep part of the diversification curve.

Why this is correct: At 50 stocks, the investor has already eliminated most idiosyncratic (unsystematic) risk. The marginal benefit of adding more stocks follows a law of diminishing returns—each new stock contributes less risk reduction than the previous one. Moving from 50 to 60 stocks therefore produces only a marginal decrease in portfolio risk.

Why the others are wrong: A) Assumes a linear relationship between stock count and risk reduction. Risk reduction is non-linear; a 20% increase in stocks does not produce a 20% decrease in risk, especially at larger portfolio sizes. C) Treats diversification as monotonically beneficial without limit. In reality, the benefit curve flattens sharply after ~25–30 stocks; adding beyond this point yields minimal further risk reduction. D) Confuses the types of risk. While systematic risk (beta-driven) cannot be diversified away, unsystematic risk absolutely can be—and the question concerns the risk-reduction effect of adding stocks, which is primarily a diversification play.

Intuition: In equity research, practitioners recognize that a 30–50 stock portfolio is the practical sweet spot. Beyond this, the effort to source and monitor additional holdings yields minimal risk reduction and often introduces operational drag. This insight guides portfolio construction and rebalancing decisions.
